content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe how temperature affects reaction rate
Explain the effect using collision theory and energy distribution
Design experiments to investigate temperature effects

Temperature has a dramatic effect on reaction rate. A small increase in temperature can cause a large increase in rate. This is why we refrigerate food (to slow decomposition) and cook food at high temperatures (to speed up chemical changes).
Increasing temperature increases the rate of reaction.
For every 10°C rise in temperature, the rate approximately doubles.
This is a much larger effect than concentration - temperature has a dramatic impact on rate.
Two reasons why higher temperature increases rate:
Higher temperature = particles have more kinetic energy
At higher temperature, particles collide with more energy
A greater proportion of collisions have energy ≥ activation energy
This is the major reason for the large effect
Explore the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution — see how temperature affects the spread of particle energies using the interactive visualisation below.
shows how particle energies are distributed in a sample.
[DIAGRAM: Maxwell-Boltzmann curves at two temperatures (T1 and T2 where T2 > T1) with activation energy marked]
Few particles have very low or very high energies
The area under the curve to the right of Eₐ = particles that can react
At higher temperature, the curve shifts right and flattens
Much larger area beyond Eₐ at higher temperature
Why Temperature Has Such a Large Effect
Small fraction of particles have energy ≥ Eₐ
Much larger fraction have energy ≥ Eₐ
The increase in successful collisions is much greater than the increase in collision frequency.
Volume vs time at different temperatures:
All reach same final volume (same amount of reactant)
Heat sodium thiosulfate solution to required temperature
Place flask on paper with cross
Add acid (at same temperature) and start timer
Record time for cross to disappear
Each 10°C increase approximately halves the time
Use a water bath for accurate temperature control
Allow time for temperature to stabilize
Measure temperature at start of reaction
Difficult for exothermic reactions (they heat up)
Use large volumes or water bath to minimize temperature change
Use collision theory to explain why a 10°C temperature increase approximately doubles the reaction rate.
At higher temperature, particles have more kinetic energy
They move faster, so there are more collisions per second (minor effect)
More importantly, collisions are more energetic
Looking at the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, a small temperature increase shifts the curve significantly to the right
The area beyond Eₐ (particles with enough energy to react) roughly doubles
This means the proportion of successful collisions roughly doubles
Use the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution to explain why catalysts increase rate.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy (Eₐ)
On the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, this moves the Eₐ line to the left
A larger area of the curve is now to the right of Eₐ
More particles have sufficient energy to react
(Note: the curve itself doesn't change - only where Eₐ is)
A reaction takes 80 seconds at 25°C. Estimate how long it would take at 35°C.
At 20°C, a reaction has rate 0.5 mol/s. Estimate the rate at 40°C.
Saying particles gain kinetic energy and collide more often (incomplete)
The main reason is more energetic collisions, not just more frequent ones
Drawing Maxwell-Boltzmann curves that cross at the peak
Higher temperature curve is lower and broader (flattened)
Both reactant solutions should be at the test temperature
Particles move faster (more collisions) - minor effect
Collisions more energetic (more exceed Eₐ) - major effect
Practical: use water bath, pre-heat solutions, control variables
